hook: Sarah Bird earned a BS in computer engineering from the University of Texas at Austin in 2007, where as an undergraduate she worked through a co-op program at IBM contributing to the design of the Xbox 360 processor chip. She went on to earn a PhD in computer science from UC Berkeley, advised by Dave Patterson alongside Krste Asanović and Burton Smith. She became a founding member of the AI ethics group at Facebook, now Meta, before moving to Microsoft, where in 2017 she established the company's first research group dedicated to AI ethics, later growing into the FATE research group. As Chief Product Officer of Responsible AI at Microsoft, she leads the team responsible for identifying emerging AI risks and building mitigation tools, and guided the responsible development of products including GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Copilot. Her team has also released open source tools such as Fairlearn and, more recently, the ASSERT safety evaluation tool and the Agent Control Specification governance standard.

standing.watch: Both cases on the site remain unresolved. In The New York Times Co. v. Microsoft Corp. and OpenAI, the record shows discovery and summary judgment briefing closed April 2, 2026, and the case was consolidated into MDL 1:25-md-03143 as of 2026-09-24. Authors Guild v. OpenAI, Inc. is a class action in discovery, consolidated into the same MDL before Judge Stein as of 2026-09-24. Neither case names Bird, and the records do not connect the two cases to her work directly. Beyond the recent release of ASSERT and the Agent Control Specification, the records say nothing about what her team plans next.
standing.record: The records trace a path from hardware to ethics and product governance. Bird earned a BS in computer engineering from the University of Texas at Austin in 2007, and as an undergraduate she worked through a co-op program at IBM contributing to the design of the Xbox 360 processor chip. She then earned a PhD in computer science at UC Berkeley, advised by Dave Patterson alongside Krste Asanović and Burton Smith. Before Microsoft she was a founding member of the AI ethics group at Facebook, now Meta. The site lists one company for her, Microsoft, and two lawsuits, The New York Times Co. v. Microsoft Corp. and OpenAI and Authors Guild v. OpenAI, Inc., neither of which names her personally. The pattern is a career spent building the governance layer around AI products rather than the products alone.
standing.standing: Sarah Bird is Chief Product Officer of Responsible AI at Microsoft, the only company the site lists her as an executive of. In that role she leads the team responsible for identifying emerging AI risks and building mitigation tools, according to the records. She established Microsoft's first research group dedicated to AI ethics in 2017, and that group later grew into the FATE research group. She guided the responsible development of GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Copilot. Her team has released open source tools including Fairlearn, and more recently the ASSERT safety evaluation tool and the Agent Control Specification governance standard. Her influence therefore runs through both Microsoft's flagship AI products and the public tooling her team puts out.
